newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian employers urge lower EU payments.
newsitem.headline: Austrian employers urge lower EU payments.

text.p: Austria's Chamber of Economy said on Tuesday EU membership had brought enormous benefits but it argued that Vienna's contributions to Brussels should be reduced or frozen.
Walter Ertl, who heads the trade section of the employers' association, told journalists the countdown to a single European currency was putting enormous pressure on member states' budgets.
"I see a trend towards freezing contributions. Given a rising GDP that would represent a reduction in real terms," Ertl said.
Austria, which joined the EU on January 1 last year, contributed 25.6 billion schillings to Brussels in its first year of membership.
Some 10.1 billion schillings flowed back in subsidies and other payments but only 1.1 billion schillings found their way to central government.

"The net burden on (the central government's) budget was 48.7 billion schillings," Ertl said, pointing to additional entry expenses of 7.7 billion schillings and costs of 16.5 billion schillings associated with switching to EU tax systems.
Ertl rated low consumer price inflation and booming foreign investment as the biggest advantages of EU membership.

He said foreign firms had invested 31.2 billion schillings since the start of last year, excluding foreign participation in Bank Austria and Bank fuer Arbeit und Wirtschaft AG (BAWAG) and the sale of the Billa supermarket chain to Germany's Rewe.
Austrian annual inflation slowed to 1.8 percent in August from 2.1 percent the previous year.
"Without the EU..that would not have been possible," Ertl said.
He said the credibility of a future single European currency would depend on the participants and expressed the hope that Italy would make the start.
The chamber also expressed some reservations about the proposed eastward expansion of the economic bloc.
"That can only be financed if we carry on with existing fund structures and lower the criteria. Otherwise all the new states will qualify for high levels of subsidies," Ertl said.
